utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. First of all, our apologies for the delayed start. We had some technical problems with the lines set up for the videolink to Belgrade. As you can see here, only two Judges present. Judge Nyambe couldn't make it to take part due to another commitment, so the Chamber decided to sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis. I know that we have to deal with some procedural matters, but we should do that at the end of today's hearing and to start with the witness. Sir, the Chamber's grateful that you are able to be in that place where we can have this videolink and that you are able to provide us with your knowledge about certain instances. I would like to invite you to indicate if you have any medical problems that you need a break, an earlier break, or a rest, please let us know if that is the cases. Now please rise and read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you by Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Sir, first the Prosecutor is putting questions to you during his examination-in-chief, followed by Mr. Tolimir during his cross-examination. Mr. Elderkin, you have the floor. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honour Judge Mindua, and to everyone else in the courtroom here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness and the staff over in Sarajevo. Witness, as you know, my name is Rupert Elderkin. I hope, first, that you're able to hear me clearly, and if at any time you can't hear my questions through interpretation or there's any other problem, then please let us know. I'm going to ask, please, for you to saw your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Very well. My name is Ramiz Dumanjic. I was born in Rogatica in 1943 and I lived and worked there as an imam, as a religious cleric in a village up until 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Dumanjic, could I ask you to stop for one second? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: And because of the fighting that had started there already in April of 1992, I went to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Excuse me for a moment, Mr. Dumanjic, please.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: And I stayed there until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I wanted to interrupt you because we are going to take the story of your time in Zepa step-by-step, and it's important for me to be able to ask you questions for which you can answer each question in turn. I know you're keen to get through the story, and we'll go as quickly as possible, but if you could just answer the questions I ask in that sequence it will help us here to follow your story and also to have a good written record of your evidence today. So I've heard your brief summary of your background and that you were in Zepa during the wartime period, but I'd like to first ask you: Do you remember being interviewed and giving a witness statement a couple of months ago at your home in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did you listen as an interpreter read the statement to you by telephone in your own language and you were able to check that the information was correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did you sign a paper copy of the statement once you had made any corrections?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And were you happy when you signed the statement that the contents were true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay. So if there is anything today you have trouble remembering, then we can show you that statement if it does help you to remember any of the facts. I think you've told us already that you were an imam and that you grew up in Rogatica before the war. Can I just confirm that's correct, please?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And I think you also said you were living in Rogatica at the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, in a village near Rogatica, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You've also told us that you went to Zepa in April of 1992. Can you tell us, please, why you moved to Zepa at that time?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I -- my wife hailed from Zepa, and there was a vacant post for an imam over there, and I went there for work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you stay in Zepa during the period from 1992 onwards?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Was there any reason why you didn't return to your home near Rogatica, having moved to Zepa in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: But of course there was. I was unable to return there because of the fighting. I didn't dare to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Why didn't you dare to return, sir? What were you afraid of if you tried to return to the Rogatica area?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: When exactly do you mean, after the war or during the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: During the war, sir.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I was unable to go back there because of the armed activities taking place there. There were no people to be an imam to. The mosque had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: While you were in Zepa, where were you living?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I lived in a flat belonging to the municipality right next to the mosque. It was allocated or set aside for an imam to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And to be clear, just so we can locate that, is that the mosque in Zepa town itself?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: In the very centre of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, were you in the military at any point during your time in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I was not. I was performing my religious duties and was therefore free of any war assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Please could you describe for us what were your religious duties during that period.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I performed religious services five times a day. I also officiated at funerals, and there were quite a few of those, and I was also engaged in religious teaching. That was all, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When you were in Zepa, did you know a person named Mehmed Hajric?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a colleague of mine. We worked together. When Podzeplje fell, where he served, he came to Zepa, and from then on we worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you remember around what date Podzeplje fell and Mr. Hajric came to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Right away in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know why he left Podzeplje? Why didn't he just stay living in Podzeplje?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Because of combat activities. All the population from Podzeplje came to Zepa, and he followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When you say "all the population from Podzeplje came to Zepa," what ethnicity was that population? Are you talking about Serbs, Bosnian Muslims, or some other population group?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: There were Muslims in Podzeplje. However, they were driven out by the Serbian Army and were forced to come over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What were the duties that Mr. Hajric performed while he was an imam in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: He was giving religious instruction to children, and we also performed religious services alternately. We would take turns for the Friday prayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you remember if he performed any work other than his duties as imam?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about Hajric?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Yes, please. I'm talking about Mr. Hajric.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Later on in 1993, Hajric also worked in the municipality. It was the war municipality of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Hajric is still alive?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Hajric is alive today?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: No. He was killed in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the circumstances of his death?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: The only thing I know is that UNPROFOR forces took him over, and from there the Serbian Army took him to the Rogatica camp. He had even been registered by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat the last part of his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, could you please repeat the last part of your answer. It was not properly understood by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbian Army seized him from the UNPROFOR personnel and transferred him to the Rogatica camp. There he was registered by the Red Cross, and subsequently they killed him under the pretext that he had attempted to flee, to break away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know when this killing took place?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I wasn't a participant in these events. I heard it from his father. He told me the story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment. We have to interrupt you. I'm sorry for that. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. Tolimir has technical difficulties. He can't hear either the questions or the answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did that -- did that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tolimir is receiving only the English interpretation, whereas the Serbian is completely drowned out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was that the case from the beginning of the testimony of the witness or did it just happen? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry? Beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, was that the case from the beginning of the testimony, or did it happen just now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that it has been present for a while, the difficulty. He hasn't been able to hear the answers to the questions for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'm being asked to say something to see if the interpretation is now coming through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, first of all, I would like to invite you -- Mr. Tolimir, are you hearing me? Do you receive B/C/S translation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I am receiving interpretation of your words. I'm also receiving interpretation of what Mr. Elderkin is saying in part, as well as of that which the witness is saying, but it's pretty muffled. It's like I'm hearing a muffled version of what is said in the Serbian, whereas I can hear the English perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we all know the procedure. Please interrupt again if you have a technical problem or a problem of understanding the B/C/S translation immediately when such a problem occurs again. Let just continue and see if now you are receiving better interpretation and you can hear it better. Mr. Elderkin, just continue and we will see how it works.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Dumanjic, I'm starting again with the question, so please can you indicate if you can hear us also.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You were just telling us --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me just say that I can't hear the witness. Thank you. I can't hear his answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have to make sure that Mr. Tolimir understands the witness and his answers. If there's a technical problem, we have to check it first. Mr. Elderkin, perhaps you'd put the next question -- or again the same question and try to get a longer answer so we have a chance to check the technical situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us that you learnt about Mr. Hajric's fate from his father. Do you know or have you learnt why Mr. Hajric was killed?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: The reason must have been the fact that he was an imam.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In this case, we should wait until it is set up and the technical equipment is adjusted. The technician is working on that, Mr. Tolimir. I would like to invite the witness to repeat the last answer. I'm very sorry that we have this technical problem. This occurs from time to time. We hope it will be solved very soon. Please repeat your last answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were asking me why Hajric was killed. Because he was an imam and a Muslim. There can be no other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dumanjic. I'll continue questioning only once we know that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please, we have to interrupt for a moment. If I go on the B/C/S channel, I can hear the witness, although it is not very clear, but I can understand that. The technician is working on this problem. I hope it will be resolved very soon. We have to wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Elderkin, and Mr. Dumanjic, I was told that the system is working better now, and therefore we should check if everything is okay. Mr. Elderkin, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Dumanjic, I would like to ask now if during your time in Zepa you knew a person named Fehim Alispahic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Please could you tell us who he was.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: He was an imam from Vlahovici who also came to Zepa and assisted us in our work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, did you -- did you understand the last answer?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I understood it all. The only thing that was not clear was whether the village was Vlahovici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vlahovici. That's in the Visegrad municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You may continue, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, do you know where the village of Vlahovici is located in relation to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Well, I know. I was there once as a young man. There were Bajram festivities going on there, so I had an occasion to visit the place, and I knew that there was a mosque there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us where it is located? Is it in Visegrad municipality, Rogatica municipality? What kind of distance is it from Zepa, please?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: It's in the municipality of Visegrad, close to Zepa. Right across the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Mr. Alispahic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Well, the same. The Serbian Army drove out the villagers of that village, and he joined others in coming to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know if he managed to leave Zepa when the enclave fell in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did manage to leave. He probably got on a bus. He was an elderly man. Several years later, he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, did you know during your time in Zepa a person named Jusuf Jusupovic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I did. He was a madrasa student who also assisted us in our work, particularly in giving religious instruction to children.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him when the enclave fell in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: He went across the woodland to Sarajevo. He graduated from a madrasa there, and later on got an employment with the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, were you yourself in Zepa in July 1995? Mr. Dumanjic, were you in Zepa in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was, until it fell, and I went across by bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What was the reason why you left Zepa? Why didn't you carry on living in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: You mean afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Why didn't you --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: After the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: At the time in July 1995 when you actually left, what do you think would have happened if you'd stayed living in Zepa after the Serbs took over the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Well, who would I have been an imam to since all the Muslims were driven out of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you remember -- do you remember on what date you left Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: The 27th of June -- or, rather, July 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Dumanjic, I have to interrupt you. There's a problem again. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can hear the interpreters translating into English and into B/C/S but very quietly, and I could hardly hear anything just before you said that we had to do something about that. So it seems that there is something wrong with the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I will check with the registry. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The technician is working on that problem again. Mr. Tolimir, did you do anything with the -- the technical equipment in front of you? Perhaps -- did you do something? Turn up or turn down the loudspeaker? In fact, you shouldn't. Mr. Tolimir, did you receive interpretation of what I have said?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can hear very good what is being interpreted, but a while ago the sound was not good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Elderkin, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Dumanjic, let's try and carry on. Sir, can we just ask you to repeat the date when you said that you left Zepa. I can see it says first the 27th of June on our screens here and then corrected to July. Could you please repeat that for the record.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: 27th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, would it help to remind you of the date you gave in the witness statement, because that was one day different. It was the 26th of July that you told us in that witness statement. Do you have a very clear memory of that date?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Well, it is possible. I'm not quite sure whether it was the 26th or the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How did you leave Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I set off on foot through the forest with all the other people. However, I realised that I wouldn't be able to proceed. I had very bad footwear. And then I saw buses coming to collect the people. At that point I decided to join them and to proceed by bus and that's how I crossed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could you describe to us the scene when you were getting onto the bus that you boarded, the people who were around, what you actually did.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: We boarded the buses. There was an observer from the United Nations. Since there was no seat available on the bus, I went to the back of the bus and sat down on my bag. When we arrived at Boksanica, which is above Zepa, we were stopped there. Mr. Mladic boarded the bus with a film crew and some other people in his escort, and he introduced himself to us by saying, "Do you know who I am?" We said, "No." He said, "My name is General Mladic. The town -- the time has come for us to get acquainted. Are there any here able-bodied men?" We said there weren't. Then he said, "You go over there and join your people, but I will find them -- you there as well." I understood that to be a threat addressed to us Muslims in the sense that we had no place at all in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, what was the atmosphere like on the bus among the passengers when General Mladic was speaking to you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Well, it was very difficult. I was terrified, because I thought that they were going to take me off the bus. Other people were frightened too. However, when Mladic said that, "We're not going to bring any harm to you. Go ahead and join your people," we said, "Thank you, General." After that, the bus --

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Let me interrupt for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: -- proceeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Dumanjic, did anyone check your identity while you were on the bus?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Well, no. And even if they had done that, I had thrown away my identity card, because I feared that I would be taken off once they find out my identity. So I decided if asked, I would give them a false name and a false date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Why were you afraid that you would be taken off if those checking your identity found out who you were? What was the reason for that fear?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Because I was an imam. I know from experience what they did elsewhere, that they particularly made a point of taking imams to camps and killing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: While you were on the bus and leaving from Zepa town to go up to Boksanica, what did you see as you drove along the road up to Boksanica?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I saw houses ablaze. Some were almost burned completely. I saw many Serbian soldiers by the road who were rejoicing at us being taken out of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know who had set the houses ablaze?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: The Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, if you could continue, please, for the journey after Boksanica. Where did the bus take you after that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: We reached the so-called Saversko [phoen] then Rogatica. We saw Serb civilians gathering hay, and these people really didn't react in any way whatsoever. They were just going about their business. It was peaceful when we arrived in Rogatica. Then we went on to Sokolac, and we had no problems there until we arrived in Han Pijesak. The bus driver stopped at the petrol station, claiming that he had a puncture, but that was not correct. At that point, a young man boarded the bus, and there was a man called Omer sitting in the front. The young man slapped him on the face, shouting, "All these people should be killed." I got terrified at that moment. However, the Serbian police arrived, and they really acted in a correct and proper way. They chased away this young man, and we were able to proceed, which we did later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where did you finally get off the bus?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: There were no more problems. We headed off to Kladanj, but before that there was a place called Luka. This is where we disembarked from the buses and proceeded on foot. However, there were quite a few roadblocks on the way. At one of the roadblocks, two or three Serbian soldiers approached us. One of them asked me for money. He just said, "Uncle, give me some money." And I said, "I have no money. I didn't work for money." He saw that I had a wallet in my pocket. He took it out and found $10 in it. This money had been given to me by a man for whom I performed funeral services. He returned the wallet back to my pocket and said, "Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Apart from that indent, did you see anything else that you remember after you got off the bus and started walking?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the way, I was able to see that. While we were walking, we saw many dead bodies covered with blankets.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, did your family also leave Zepa at the end of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: They remained behind in Zepa. They spent the night there and then joined me on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, thank you very much. I don't have any further questions for you now, but other people will.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. Witness, on page 15 of today's transcript, line 10 to 12 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no translation into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A technical problem. Would Judge Mindua kindly repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to start again. Witness, Witness Dumanjic, on page 15 of today's transcript, lines 10 to 12, you stated that when you were in Boksanica on the bus, you were very afraid because you were an imam and because experience had told you that everywhere else imams were captured and transferred to camps to be killed. The question I wish to put to you is this: When you were on board that bus at that very moment, had you learned that imams had been killed, or did you learn that after the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I had experience. I heard on the radio that the imam of Semizovac had been killed in 1992 alongside his whole family. Then there was another case in Visegrad. In the village of Okrug, an imam was also killed. So these are the things that I heard on the radio. It was on the news.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you, Witness. Thank you, Mr. Dumanjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Dumanjic, I have also a question for you. You described the situation at the Boksanica check-point when the buses were stopped, and you told us that General Mladic, together with a film team, entered the bus, the bus you were in. Can you please again tell us what General Mladic told the people on the bus? What exactly did he say?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: He identified himself by saying, "I am General Mladic. The time has come for us to meet." He inquired whether there were any able-bodied men. We said there weren't, to which he retorted, "You just proceed and join your people, but rest assured that we are going to find you there as well."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Dumanjic, now Mr. Tolimir has the opportunity to put questions to you during his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Greetings to all present in the court and in the courtroom in Sarajevo where the witness and the Prosecutor are sitting, as well as a representative of the registry. I wish peace upon everyone who is following this broadcast, and I would prefer these proceedings to be completed in accordance with providence and not in accordance with my wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dumanjic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One correction. Where the witness is situated there is no Prosecutor. There is a member of the Registry to assist him, just for the record. Now put your question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I stood corrected when I said the representative of the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, we all are experiencing the same noise. It disappeared. Now, please try to put your question to the witness, Mr. Tolimir. You have the floor again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Dumanjic, in order to make thing easier for you, we're going to go chronologically according to the answers that you gave, and I only have a few questions for you. Can you tell me, please, when the Judge asked you about what General Mladic said when he boarded the bus and you said that he wanted to know whether there were any able-bodied men among you, the people on the bus said that there weren't, and then he said, "Go and join your people, we are going to find you." My question is: Were any able bodies men on the bus; that is to say, the people who were subject to military obligation under the law?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: No. No, there were not such people. There were only elderly people, women, and children on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us did you fall into the category of able-bodied men, because you had an assignment before the war in Han Pijesak? Can you tell us again the year in which you were born, and please wait until everything that I asked you is recorded in the transcript, because we both speak the same language.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1943, and I don't know for how long one is subject to military obligation, and I don't know whether I was in that category or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we speak the same language, I asked you to wait a little until I have finished my question, and I shall do the same for you. This will allow the court reporter to record everything in the transcript, the question and the answer.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: All right. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber how old were you in 1995, since you said you were born in 1943? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: 1943. Well, you can do the arithmetic yourself. I can't be bothered. I am an ill man.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please once again make a pause after my question so that everything can be properly recorded, because otherwise we have overlapping between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. This is the first time I'm doing this, and I'm not very experienced. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I sometimes make the same mistakes as well. All right. Now the interpretation is finished. Can you tell us, please, were people of 52 years of age, which was your age when you left Zepa, were they conscripts and were they subject to respond to military according to the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina and also of Republika Srpska? Do you know how these issues were regulated?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the provisions of the law were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me for asking you this. I think you would have known this, because you were a conscript.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but before the war. But a few years before the war I was relieved of that obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, on page 4 of today's transcript, line 14, Mr. Elderkin, the Prosecutor, asked you why you didn't go back to Rogatica from Zepa. Before that, you said that you went to Zepa to take the vacancy of the imam that was open there and that there was another reason which was that your wife was originally from Zepa.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I went there because there was a vacancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is the following: If you took the job of a religious person in Zepa, were you able at the same time to go back and perform other duties or become involved in other profession elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Are you referring to the period after the war when you speak about my returning to Zep?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question was: Were you able to perform the duties of an imam in Rogatica at a time while you were appointed imam in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't do that. Once I made a commitment, that's what I remained working.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now the sound has disappeared. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Dumanjic, tell us, please, was any person on board the bus checked by the Army of Republika Srpska, and I'm talking about their identity. I am also talking about your journey from Zepa to other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that was not the case, although I expected it to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As you say, you tried to cross the mountain from Zepa on foot. Can you tell us how many people you saw there getting ready to cross the Zepa mountain on foot to the territory under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I did try to get out of the area across the mountain, but I didn't manage to. The slope was steep, and I decided to return right away and board a bus, so I didn't see any of the people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As an imam, were you aware of any individuals taking off the -- being taken off the bus that was headed for Zepa and kept behind in that area under the territory of the Army of Republika Srpska contrary to international conventions?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: None of the people who were there on the bus with me were taken off. However, the bus that my wife and children boarded, who followed me a day later from Zepa, certain individuals were taken off the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me about that last bus that your wife boarded? How many individuals were taken off, and were they able-bodied men? Were they conscripts? Did they fall within that category of individuals or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: They were elderly people. They were not military-age men. I know some of them. One from Srebrenica, some from Vlahovici who were also taken off and held at the Rogatica camp for some five or six months. They joined us at a later date. I don't know how many in all there were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at P1434, please. It's a list of individuals who were taken on by the Rogatica reception centre that you call a camp. And please have a look at the list and see if there are any elderly people among them, or if these individuals fell into the category of able-bodied men. It's tab 6, and it's one of the documents you have before you. Have a look at the document and tell us whether any of these individuals were elderly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: There's one individual I know, Mehmed Prcic. I know him too.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know him too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, could you please repeat the name --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Saban, whom I also know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the names of those you are familiar with.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you please again say the name, because the interpreters didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bego. Zecir Batres. Nurbeg Gladovic. Omer Cavcic. Edhem Brguilja. Omer Delic. Nirzim [phoen] Otalagic. Ahmed Brguilja. Those are the ones I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise for bothering you with looking through the names. Now, tell us, please, the individuals that you referred to as the ones that you know, were they exchanged? In other words, did you see them later, did you hear of them, were they able to reach the free territory of the Federation of Bosnia Herzegovina? And I'm referring to the individuals whose names you just read out.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if they were exchanged or just simply released. I don't have any knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, do you know if the individuals who boarded the last bus were taken off because they did not comply with the agreement that was signed based on which all the able-bodied men were supposed to be disarmed by UNPROFOR in Zepa; in other words, give their weapons over to them before they cross over to the territory of the federation? Were you aware of this at all?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can we now call up P736. Please familiarise yourself with the contents. It was written on the 27th of July, 1995, and signed by, on behalf of the Serbian side Mr. Rajko Kusic, and on behalf of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mehmed Mahic, Hamdija Torlak, and Amir Imamovic, and General Mladic also signed it as a witness to that agreement, and it was also supposed to be signed by a representative of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should stop for a moment because the transcript is not working. It stopped when you asked for a certain document number. We need the assistance of a technician. Mr. Tolimir, please repeat your full question, because it was not recorded, what was said, until you called up the document. Please once again. Now the transcript is working.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: After having called document P736, I said: Mr. Dumanjic, do you know why the last bus which your wife boarded was pulled over and why certain men were taken off? Did it have anything to do with the fact that the Muslims did not honour the agreement that they had signed about disarming their own men and handing over the weapons to the UNPROFOR personnel in centre of Zepa? Thank you. That was my question, Mr. Dumanjic. Now, in the meantime, Mr. Dumanjic was able to read the document and is now able to answer my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I did read the document, and I believe that none of the parties complied with the agreement, neither your side, nor the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dumanjic. Can you specifically indicate the part which the Serbian side supposedly did in the adhere to?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Well, here's an example for you. The brothers Gladovic are elderly men who were taken off the bus. They were no conscripts at all. They were elderly individuals. And besides, if Mehmed Hajric complied with this agreement, why was he killed? He was not supposed to have been killed. He was supposed to have been exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dumanjic. My question for you was this: Were all men taken off the bus, and I emphasise "men," after it came to be known that the men present in the Zepa mountains did not wish to surrender themselves and be disarmed before being transferred to the territory of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina? You gave us the answer you wanted to give us, and that is it.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm clear on the question at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, then I'll repeat it. Had the able-bodied men at the -- in the Zepa mountains surrendered themselves and had they turned their weapons over to UNPROFOR and had they complied with the provisions of the agreement whereby UNPROFOR was supposed to transfer them from Zepa to the territory under the control of the BH Army, would any of the individuals who were on that bus have been taken prisoner or killed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment. I interrupt you, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tolimir, is it your opinion that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You may answer in a moment, but Mr. Elderkin gets the floor first. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would object to that last question. It's asking a hypothetical. It's not asking about matters that are actually within the witness's actual possible knowledge. It's rephrased about what actually happened or what he believed, that's one thing, but to ask him a long compound question about what might have happened in another set of events isn't -- isn't appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, not only the last question was quite complicated because you put together many things, please put very simple questions to the witness and one by one. Please rephrase your last question, and only one question at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, and thank you to Mr. Elderkin for his assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can the witness please say the following: There were individuals who boarded the buses, but would they not have been allowed to reach the point of the free territory of the BH Federation had those who were in the Zepa mountains agreed to surrender and be disarmed?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Well, do you, Mr. Tolimir, truly believe that they would have been safely transferred to the territory under the BH control? In my view, this would not have come about. They would have been killed. Otherwise, why would there have been cases of individuals being transferred to Serbia and then held in various camps over there? You know how these things turned out, don't you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, same objection, and with a very clear reason why the question is objectionable. The answer is also now hypothetical. The record is not advancing General Tolimir's case or informing us about what was actually happening within the witness's knowledge. Could we please stick to the facts rather than what might have happened in various other circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should put questions to those areas that the witness can really answer and provide you with his personal knowledge. Try to do that. Please, continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The witness did know that there were able-bodied men in the Zepa mountains. He even tried to join them. He said so in his statement. That's why I put my question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, put the next simple questions related to his knowledge, no discussion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it was only natural. We simply had to flee the area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Let me put the next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know that the government in Sarajevo negotiated the transfer of the able-bodied individuals from the Zepa mountains to Serbia and that they did not arrive in Serbia as an enemy but that they were, in fact, received by the Serbian government? Were you aware of this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, from what I heard from those who were sent to Serbia, they went there of their own will, and they were met there by the Serbian Army and put in a camp. There was no arrangement about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dumanjic. Do you know that before this Trial Chamber -- Chamber, the then UNPROFOR commander, General Smith, stated that there had been an agreement reached between Carl Bildt and Slobodan Milosevic whereby all the able-bodied men present in the Zepa mountains were to be transferred to Serbia, which would guarantee safety and security for them? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: That -- that I don't know. What I do know that during his trial, Slobodan Milosevic bragged about having saved these Muslims and did not allow them to return to the area but, rather, sent them across the world to be resettled there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, one observation. For sure this Mr. Witness was not present during the negotiations between Carl Bildt and Slobodan Milosevic. You should really focus on what this witness can provide you with. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: In addition, I'd ask for a cite for any reference to such prior testimony in the case. I'm not entirely familiar with the summary that General Tolimir has given to us there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You may leave it like this and continue with those areas of the personal knowledge of Mr. Dumanjic, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I asked him if he knew anything that. He himself said that this was being discussed at the Milosevic trial. I may refrain from asking any questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You -- you -- I don't know what the purpose of a testimony of this witness about the Milosevic trial is. He may have heard something about that trial. This is at least hearsay. You should take into account the personal situation of this witness. You know about it, and you should focus on his experience on the ground and what he observed at that time in 1995. This is now the last question before the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wanted to show a film to the witness showing the bus on which he was and all the men are there. However, my intention is not to be offensive either to the witness, to the Prosecutor, or to the Bench, and I apologise for that, and as a result, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, if you're intention is to show a video, you may do that. My intervention was related to the negotiations between Carl Bildt and Slobodan Milosevic. This can't be a reason for the conclusion of your examination. If you want to show this video to the witness, you should do that. If it's a lengthy one, perhaps we should do that after the break. Otherwise, if it's a short part of it, we can do it now if you intend to conclude your cross-examination quite soon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm grateful to Mr. Dumanjic for his answers, and I apologise to you, perhaps, for putting some questions that I shouldn't have. I'm not going to show the video, and with this I conclude the examination of this witness, and I would like to thank everyone present here in the courtroom and everyone following these proceedings. I wish him good health and God bless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. For the record, it is very clear that you have still the right to continue your cross-examination. It's your free will to conclude it now. I take it that on your own decision you conclude it now, your cross-examination. Mr. Elderkin, do you have questions during your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, just on one point, and it can be very brief, and it's in -- actually, it's a follow-up to the question that Judge Mindua asked about whether the witness, at the time he was leaving Zepa, knew about the fates of the other imams because he'd said that he heard that other imams had been imprisoned or killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Dumanjic, my question is in relation to what you said you had heard about other imams being imprisoned or killed during the war. You mentioned the imam of Semizovac and Okrug. Did you have any information or do you have any information as to how those men were captured or killed and by whom they may have been captured or killed?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question -- or, rather, I didn't hear it clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Dumanjic, do you understand me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, please put your question again, perhaps in a very simple way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, you spoke earlier about imams from two places being captured or killed. Those places were Semizovac and Okrug. Do you remember mentioning those places and people?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I mentioned it during your examination. However, it's not mentioned in my statement, because nobody asked me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of the imams of those places?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: The name of the one from Semizovac, I heard it on the radio. His last name was Ramic. I don't know his first name. And the one from Okrug was called Ramic, but I also don't know his first name.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are not quite sure that we heard the names properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you one more time to repeat those names just so that the interpreters can hear them as best possible, please?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know their first names. I only know their surnames. The one from Semizovac was Ramic, and the one from the village of Okrug near Visegrad was Karaman and that's all you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know who captured or killed either of those men? Do you know anything about their circumstances or their fate?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: The one from Semizovac was simply picked up, he and his family, and were then killed. And as for the one from Okrug, I don't know how he lost his life.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: The imam from Semizovac, you say he and his family were picked up and killed. Do you know who were the people who picked that family and that imam up and killed them? Not personally, but do you know whether they were military men? Were they civilians, police? Do you have any information at all about them?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ DUMANJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was done by the Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. Dumanjic, thank you very much. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that finishes my re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Dumanjic, the Chamber is very grateful that you were able to come to that location --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- and testify and to provide us with your knowledge about the events in 1995. Thank you very much again. It was a great help for us, and the Chamber would like to wish you all the best for your health and for your future. Thank you very much again. This concludes now your examination. I would like to say good-bye and all the best for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and I wish all the best to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, and this concludes the videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we have some minutes left. We should try to manage the procedural matters before a possible break, to save some time. I have -- I would like to raise two things. The first matter is the following: On the 7th September 2011, the Chamber granted the Prosecution's motion. It was 2011. The Prosecution's motion for the admission of the written evidence of Behara Krdzic pursuant to Rule 92 bis. In accordance with that decision, the Chamber hereby orders the Prosecution to upload the written evidence contained in annex A of that motion to e-court under a new 65 ter number. My second issue is the following: We discussed at length the admission of portions of the document D74. Mr. Gajic, for the Defence, indicated which pages should be translated and admitted into evidence. This -- now I can state these pages listed in the e-mail from Mr. Gajic will be marked for identification pending translations of these documents -- of these pages. These are the two things I wanted to raise. Are there any other matters? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in the meantime, translations arrived for the documents that were marked for identification, and with your leave, I would like to read the numbers of these documents. There's a total of ten of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's D187, D268, D271, D304, D306, D310, D311, D312, D316, and D317.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. They will now be admitted into evidence with these exhibit numbers. Are there any other matters? Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a similar list from the Prosecution with a couple of comments. The following exhibits of previously MFI'd, the translations are now uploaded: P898, P2404, P2451, P2586. In relation to P2404, Your Honours, this is an OTP interview with a protected witness. The B/C/S that's uploaded is complete, but the English transcript at the moment is missing the last 29 pages. It happens to have been a two-part document, and the Prosecution would request permission to add those pages to match the full -- full B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Leave is granted to add these pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And in addition, there are two exhibits, P2662 and P2663. These are two of the intercept handwritten notebooks, and we'd ask that they be marked as confidential. I understand that they are currently not marked as such, but they're the handwritten documents which I think have some identifying features of protected witnesses in them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I take it they are already in evidence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: P2662 is in evidence, and P2663 is also in evidence, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't see a problem, and I don't see an objection. These two documents, P2662 and P2663, will be put under seal. The other documents previously marked for identification pending translation will now be received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't see any reason for further discussion of procedural matters. As the parties are aware, we are looking forward to another witness arriving and testifying here in the courtroom. We don't know exactly when, but it may happen -- perhaps at the beginning of next week. You should be aware we will communicate the proper date as soon as possible, perhaps today or at least tomorrow. Please be prepared for this examination. We have to adjourn sine die, but we will announce the next day of hearings as soon as possible. We adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: at 11.24 a.m. sine die
